Exodus 1.summary: The book begins by naming the sons of Jacob who came to Egypt, and their family grows into a great people (Exodus 1:1–7). A new king who "knew not Joseph" fears them and makes them slaves, forcing them to build the store cities Pithom and Raamses (Exodus 1:8–14). He orders the Hebrew midwives, Shiphrah and Puah, to kill every newborn boy, but they fear God and refuse (Exodus 1:15–21). Then Pharaoh commands that every Hebrew son be thrown into the river (Exodus 1:22). This slavery is the problem the rest of the book answers.
Exodus 1.whereWeAre: Genesis ended with Jacob's family safe in Egypt and Joseph's death. Exodus picks up years later, after that family has grown into a nation. Then "there arose up a new king over Egypt, which knew not Joseph" (Exodus 1:8), and chapter 2 introduces the baby who will lead them out.

keyFigures.name: Pharaoh
keyFigures.role: The new king of Egypt, who makes Israel slaves and orders their baby boys killed.

keyFigures.name: The children of Israel
keyFigures.role: Jacob's descendants, who keep growing even as they are oppressed.

keyFigures.name: Shiphrah and Puah
keyFigures.role: Hebrew midwives who fear God and refuse to kill the boys.

keyThemes.explanation: "But the more they afflicted them, the more they multiplied and grew." Egypt cannot stop God's promise.
The midwives fear God more than the king and save the baby boys.
Pharaoh orders every Hebrew son thrown into the river, which sets up the story of Moses' rescue.

Exodus 2.summary: A Levite mother hides her baby son, then sets him in a basket among the reeds of the Nile. Pharaoh's daughter finds him, names him Moses, and raises him, while his own mother nurses him (Exodus 2:1–10). As a man, Moses kills an Egyptian who is beating a Hebrew and flees from Pharaoh to Midian (Exodus 2:11–15). There he helps the daughters of Reuel, the priest of Midian, at a well and marries Zipporah (Exodus 2:16–22). Back in Egypt, Israel groans under slavery, and God hears and remembers his covenant (Exodus 2:23–25).
Exodus 2.whereWeAre: Chapter 1 ended with Pharaoh ordering every Hebrew baby boy thrown into the Nile. This chapter tells how one of those boys, Moses, is saved and raised in Pharaoh's own palace. It ends with Moses living far away in Midian and God hearing Israel's cries, which leads to the burning bush in chapter 3.

keyFigures.name: Moses
keyFigures.role: Saved as a baby, raised by Pharaoh's daughter, and forced to flee to Midian as a man.

keyFigures.name: Moses' mother and sister
keyFigures.role: Hide the baby, watch over him, and arrange for his own mother to nurse him.

keyFigures.name: Pharaoh's daughter
keyFigures.role: Finds the baby in the river and raises him as her son.

keyFigures.name: Reuel (Jethro)
keyFigures.role: The priest of Midian, who takes Moses into his home.

keyFigures.name: Zipporah
keyFigures.role: Reuel's daughter, who marries Moses.

keyFigures.name: God
keyFigures.role: Hears Israel's groaning and remembers his covenant.

keyThemes.explanation: The baby Pharaoh wanted drowned is pulled from the river and raised in Pharaoh's own house.
Moses kills an Egyptian to help his people, but it only drives him away.
God hears Israel's groaning and remembers his covenant with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.

Exodus 3.summary: While tending Jethro's flock at Horeb, Moses sees a bush that burns but is not consumed, and God calls him to take off his shoes on holy ground (Exodus 3:1–6). God says he has seen his people's misery and is sending Moses to bring them out of Egypt (Exodus 3:7–12). When Moses asks God's name, God answers, "I AM THAT I AM" (Exodus 3:13–15). God then tells Moses to gather the elders, go to Pharaoh, and expect Egypt to send Israel away with riches (Exodus 3:16–22).
Exodus 3.whereWeAre: Moses has spent many years as a shepherd in Midian since fleeing Egypt in chapter 2. Now God meets him in a burning bush and calls him to go back and lead Israel out. Moses' doubts and objections continue into chapter 4.

keyFigures.name: God
keyFigures.role: Speaks from the burning bush, reveals his name, and sends Moses to Egypt.

keyFigures.name: Moses
keyFigures.role: Turns aside to see the bush, then argues that he is not the right man to go.

keyFigures.name: The angel of the LORD
keyFigures.role: Appears to Moses "in a flame of fire out of the midst of a bush."

keyThemes.explanation: God's presence makes the ground holy, so Moses takes off his shoes and hides his face.
God has seen his people's suffering and heard their cry, and he comes down to rescue them.
Moses feels unfit, and God's answer is his own presence: "Certainly I will be with thee."
God reveals himself as "I AM THAT I AM," the God who always is.

explainedReferences.explanation: Instruction to Moses to remove his sandals on holy ground.
Jesus references the burning-bush declaration naming the patriarchs.
Words identifying himself as God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.
Self-identification at the burning bush.

Exodus 4.summary: Moses fears that Israel will not believe him, so God gives him three signs: a rod that becomes a serpent, a hand made leprous and healed, and water turned to blood (Exodus 4:1–9). When Moses says he is slow of speech and begs God to send someone else, God sends Aaron to speak for him (Exodus 4:10–17). Moses takes his family and sets out for Egypt with "the rod of God" in his hand (Exodus 4:18–23). On the way, the LORD meets Moses and seeks to kill him until Zipporah circumcises their son (Exodus 4:24–26). Aaron meets Moses, they tell the elders everything, and the people believe and worship (Exodus 4:27–31).
Exodus 4.whereWeAre: God has just called Moses at the burning bush in chapter 3, but Moses is still not sure. God answers his fears with signs and gives him his brother Aaron as a helper. Moses heads back to Egypt, and in chapter 5 he stands before Pharaoh for the first time.

keyFigures.name: God
keyFigures.role: Gives Moses signs, grows angry at his excuses, and sends Aaron to help him.

keyFigures.name: Moses
keyFigures.role: Asks God to send someone else, then sets out for Egypt.

keyFigures.name: Aaron
keyFigures.role: Meets Moses at the mountain of God and speaks for him to the elders.

keyFigures.name: Zipporah
keyFigures.role: Circumcises her son when the LORD meets Moses on the road.

keyFigures.name: Jethro
keyFigures.role: Lets Moses go back to Egypt.

keyFigures.name: The elders of Israel
keyFigures.role: Hear the message, see the signs, and worship.

keyThemes.explanation: God gives Moses three signs so that the people will believe.
Moses says he is slow of speech, and God answers, "Who hath made man's mouth?"
The elders hear that God has seen their affliction, and they bow and worship.

Exodus 5.summary: Moses and Aaron tell Pharaoh, "Let my people go," but Pharaoh answers that he does not know the LORD (Exodus 5:1–5). He orders that the slaves gather their own straw and still make the same number of bricks (Exodus 5:6–14). The Israelite officers are beaten, and they blame Moses and Aaron (Exodus 5:15–21). Moses asks God why he has let things get worse (Exodus 5:22–23).
Exodus 5.whereWeAre: Moses and Aaron have returned to Egypt, and at the end of chapter 4 the people believed them. Now they tell Pharaoh, "Let my people go" (Exodus 5:1), and he answers by making the slaves' work harder. Moses' discouraged prayer leads into God's promises in chapter 6.

keyFigures.name: Moses and Aaron
keyFigures.role: Ask Pharaoh to let Israel go and hold a feast in the wilderness.

keyFigures.name: Pharaoh
keyFigures.role: Refuses and makes the slaves gather their own straw.

keyFigures.name: The taskmasters
keyFigures.role: Egyptian overseers who drive the people harder.

keyFigures.name: The Israelite officers
keyFigures.role: Foremen who are beaten and blame Moses and Aaron.

keyThemes.explanation: Pharaoh asks, "Who is the LORD, that I should obey his voice?" and refuses.
Pharaoh makes the slaves gather their own straw but keep the same number of bricks.
Moses brings his disappointment straight to God.

Exodus 6.summary: God answers Moses by repeating his name and his promises: he will free Israel, take them as his people, and bring them into the land (Exodus 6:1–8). The people are too crushed by their slavery to listen (Exodus 6:9). God sends Moses back to Pharaoh (Exodus 6:10–13). A family list traces Moses and Aaron through the tribe of Levi (Exodus 6:14–27), and Moses again says Pharaoh will not listen to him (Exodus 6:28–30).
Exodus 6.whereWeAre: Chapter 5 ended with Moses asking God why things have gotten worse. God answers with a string of promises: he will free Israel and make them his own people. A family list then shows where Moses and Aaron come from before the plagues begin in chapter 7.

keyFigures.name: God
keyFigures.role: Repeats his promises and sends Moses back to Pharaoh.

keyFigures.name: Moses
keyFigures.role: Tells the people God's promise, then doubts that Pharaoh will listen to him.

keyFigures.name: The children of Israel
keyFigures.role: Too crushed by slavery to listen.

keyFigures.name: Aaron
keyFigures.role: Moses' brother, sent with him to Pharaoh.

keyThemes.explanation: God promises to free Israel, make them his people, and bring them into the land.
The people are so broken by slavery that they cannot take in the promise.
The family list shows that Moses and Aaron come from a family in the tribe of Levi.

Exodus 7.summary: God tells Moses that he will harden Pharaoh's heart and bring Israel out by great judgments, and Moses, now eighty, goes to Pharaoh with Aaron (Exodus 7:1–7). Aaron's rod becomes a serpent and swallows the magicians' rods, but Pharaoh will not listen (Exodus 7:8–13). In the first plague, Aaron strikes the Nile, and its water turns to blood (Exodus 7:14–25).
Exodus 7.whereWeAre: God sends Moses and Aaron back to Pharaoh after the family list in chapter 6. Here the contest begins: Aaron's staff becomes a serpent, and the Nile turns to blood. This is the first of ten plagues, which continue through chapter 11.

keyFigures.name: God
keyFigures.role: Tells Moses he will harden Pharaoh's heart and bring Israel out with great judgments.

keyFigures.name: Moses
keyFigures.role: Goes to Pharaoh at eighty and warns him at the river.

keyFigures.name: Aaron
keyFigures.role: Throws down his rod and strikes the Nile.

keyFigures.name: Pharaoh
keyFigures.role: Hardens his heart and will not listen.

keyFigures.name: Pharaoh's magicians
keyFigures.role: Copy the first signs with their secret arts.

keyThemes.explanation: Aaron's rod swallows the magicians' rods.
The Nile, the life of Egypt, becomes blood.
Pharaoh sees the sign and still will not listen.

Exodus 8.summary: Frogs cover Egypt, and Pharaoh begs for relief, then hardens his heart once they are gone (Exodus 8:1–15). The dust becomes lice, and the magicians admit, "This is the finger of God" (Exodus 8:16–19). Swarms of flies fill Egypt but not the land of Goshen, and once again Pharaoh promises to let Israel go and then refuses (Exodus 8:20–32).
Exodus 8.whereWeAre: The Nile turned to blood in chapter 7, but Pharaoh would not listen. Now come the second, third, and fourth plagues: frogs, lice, and flies. Pharaoh promises to let Israel go and then breaks his word, and the plagues keep coming in chapter 9.

keyFigures.name: God
keyFigures.role: Sends the frogs, lice, and flies, and keeps the flies out of Goshen.

keyFigures.name: Moses
keyFigures.role: Brings God's warnings and prays for the plagues to stop.

keyFigures.name: Aaron
keyFigures.role: Stretches out his rod to bring the frogs and the lice.

keyFigures.name: Pharaoh
keyFigures.role: Promises to let Israel go, then changes his mind each time.

keyFigures.name: The magicians
keyFigures.role: Fail to make lice and say, "This is the finger of God."

keyThemes.explanation: Before each plague, Pharaoh is told to let the people go.
The magicians cannot copy the lice and admit that it is God's doing.
Each time relief comes, Pharaoh goes back on his word.

Exodus 9.summary: A disease kills the livestock of Egypt, but not one animal of Israel's dies (Exodus 9:1–7). Ashes thrown into the air bring boils on people and animals, even the magicians (Exodus 9:8–12). God warns of a terrible hail, and those who fear his word bring their servants and animals inside (Exodus 9:13–21). The hail and fire strike Egypt but not Goshen (Exodus 9:22–26). Pharaoh says, "I have sinned this time," but when the storm stops he hardens his heart again (Exodus 9:27–35).
Exodus 9.whereWeAre: Three plagues came and went in chapter 8, and Pharaoh kept going back on his word. This chapter brings the fifth, sixth, and seventh plagues: dead livestock, boils, and hail. Egypt is falling apart, but Pharaoh still refuses, which sets up the locusts and darkness in chapter 10.

keyFigures.name: God
keyFigures.role: Strikes Egypt's livestock, sends boils and hail, and spares Israel.

keyFigures.name: Moses
keyFigures.role: Throws ashes into the air, warns of the hail, and prays for it to stop.

keyFigures.name: Pharaoh
keyFigures.role: Admits "I have sinned this time," then hardens his heart again.

keyFigures.name: Pharaoh's servants
keyFigures.role: Some fear the word of the LORD and bring their servants and cattle inside.

keyFigures.name: The magicians
keyFigures.role: Cannot stand before Moses because of the boils.

keyThemes.explanation: Egypt's cattle die, but not one of Israel's.
Egyptians who fear God's word bring their servants and animals in from the hail.
Pharaoh admits his sin, but when the hail stops he hardens his heart again.

explainedReferences.explanation: Statement to Pharaoh about displaying divine power.

Exodus 10.summary: Pharaoh's own servants beg him to let Israel go, but he offers to let only the men leave (Exodus 10:1–11). Locusts cover the land and eat everything the hail left (Exodus 10:12–20). Then a thick darkness covers Egypt for three days, while Israel has light in their homes (Exodus 10:21–23). Pharaoh refuses to let the flocks go and warns Moses never to see his face again (Exodus 10:24–29).
Exodus 10.whereWeAre: Hail has just destroyed much of Egypt's crops in chapter 9. Now locusts eat what is left, and then darkness covers the land for three days. These are the eighth and ninth plagues; only one more remains, and chapter 11 announces it.

keyFigures.name: God
keyFigures.role: Sends the locusts and the darkness, while Israel has light.

keyFigures.name: Moses and Aaron
keyFigures.role: Warn Pharaoh of locusts and refuse to leave anyone behind.

keyFigures.name: Pharaoh
keyFigures.role: Offers to let only the men go, then threatens Moses' life.

keyFigures.name: Pharaoh's servants
keyFigures.role: Beg Pharaoh to let the people go before Egypt is destroyed.

keyThemes.explanation: Moses refuses to leave the children or the flocks behind.
The locusts eat everything the hail left.
Thick darkness covers Egypt for three days, but Israel has light in their homes.

Exodus 11.summary: God tells Moses that one more plague will make Pharaoh send Israel away, and the people ask the Egyptians for silver and gold (Exodus 11:1–3). Moses warns that at midnight every firstborn in Egypt will die, from Pharaoh's son to the son of a servant girl, while Israel is spared (Exodus 11:4–8). Pharaoh still will not listen, just as God said (Exodus 11:9–10).
Exodus 11.whereWeAre: Nine plagues have struck Egypt, and Pharaoh has just thrown Moses out in chapter 10. Now God announces the last and worst plague: the death of every firstborn. The chapter is a short pause before that night arrives in chapter 12.

keyFigures.name: God
keyFigures.role: Announces the last plague and gives Israel favor with the Egyptians.

keyFigures.name: Moses
keyFigures.role: Warns Pharaoh about the death of the firstborn and leaves "in a great anger."

keyFigures.name: Pharaoh
keyFigures.role: Still will not listen.

keyThemes.explanation: Moses tells Pharaoh that every firstborn in Egypt will die at midnight.
God puts a difference between Egypt and Israel, and not even a dog will bark at Israel.
The people ask the Egyptians for silver and gold, and God gives them favor.

Exodus 12.summary: God gives the Passover: each household kills a lamb, puts its blood on the doorposts, and eats the meal ready to leave, for "when I see the blood, I will pass over you" (Exodus 12:1–13). Israel is to keep the feast of unleavened bread every year to remember this day (Exodus 12:14–28). At midnight the LORD strikes the firstborn of Egypt, and Pharaoh sends Israel away (Exodus 12:29–36). About six hundred thousand men, with their families, leave Rameses after 430 years in Egypt (Exodus 12:37–42). The chapter ends with rules for who may eat the Passover (Exodus 12:43–51).
Exodus 12.whereWeAre: In chapter 11 God warned that every firstborn in Egypt would die. Here he tells Israel how to be safe: by the blood of a lamb on their doorposts. That night the plague falls, Israel finally leaves Egypt, and chapter 13 tells them how to remember it.

keyFigures.name: God
keyFigures.role: Gives the Passover and strikes down the firstborn of Egypt.

keyFigures.name: Moses and Aaron
keyFigures.role: Teach the elders the Passover and lead the people out.

keyFigures.name: The children of Israel
keyFigures.role: Put the blood on their doors, eat the meal, and leave in haste.

keyFigures.name: Pharaoh
keyFigures.role: Rises at midnight and orders Israel to go.

keyFigures.name: The Egyptians
keyFigures.role: Hurry Israel out and give them silver, gold, and clothing.

keyThemes.explanation: The lamb's blood on the door marks the homes God will pass over: "when I see the blood, I will pass over you."
Israel is to keep the Passover every year and explain it to their children.
After 430 years in Egypt, Israel walks out the same night.

explainedReferences.explanation: The requirement that none of the Passover lamb's bones be broken.

Exodus 13.summary: God claims every firstborn as his, and Moses tells the people to keep the feast and explain it to their children (Exodus 13:1–16). God leads Israel by the longer road through the wilderness, Moses carries Joseph's bones, and the LORD goes before them in a pillar of cloud by day and fire by night (Exodus 13:17–22).
Exodus 13.whereWeAre: Israel has just left Egypt on the night of the first Passover. Before the journey goes far, God tells them how to remember this day in every generation. Then he leads them by a cloud and a fire toward the sea, where chapter 14 takes place.

keyFigures.name: God
keyFigures.role: Claims the firstborn and leads Israel by a pillar of cloud and of fire.

keyFigures.name: Moses
keyFigures.role: Teaches the people to remember the day and carries Joseph's bones.

keyFigures.name: The children of Israel
keyFigures.role: Set out from Succoth for the edge of the wilderness.

keyThemes.explanation: When children ask what the feast means, parents must tell how God brought them out.
Every firstborn is set apart to the LORD to remember the night he struck Egypt's firstborn.
God takes Israel by a longer road and goes before them in cloud and fire.

explainedReferences.explanation: Consecrating every firstborn male to the Lord.

Exodus 14.summary: God leads Israel to camp by the sea, and Pharaoh chases them with six hundred chariots (Exodus 14:1–9). The people panic, but Moses says, "Fear ye not, stand still, and see the salvation of the LORD" (Exodus 14:10–14). Moses stretches out his hand, the sea divides, and Israel walks through on dry ground (Exodus 14:15–22). The waters return over the Egyptian army, and Israel fears the LORD and believes him and Moses (Exodus 14:23–31).
Exodus 14.whereWeAre: Israel left Egypt in chapter 12 and is now camped by the sea. Pharaoh changes his mind and chases them with his chariots. Moses tells the people, "stand still, and see the salvation of the LORD" (Exodus 14:13), and in chapter 15 Israel sings about what they have just seen.

keyFigures.name: God
keyFigures.role: Leads Israel to the sea, parts the waters, and overthrows the Egyptians.

keyFigures.name: Moses
keyFigures.role: Tells the people to stand still and stretches his hand over the sea.

keyFigures.name: Pharaoh and his army
keyFigures.role: Chase Israel with six hundred chariots and drown in the sea.

keyFigures.name: The children of Israel
keyFigures.role: Cry out in fear, walk through on dry ground, and believe.

keyFigures.name: The angel of God
keyFigures.role: Moves behind Israel with the pillar of cloud to guard them.

keyThemes.explanation: With the sea ahead and Pharaoh behind, Israel has no way out but God.
Moses says, "Fear ye not, stand still, and see the salvation of the LORD."
The waters return over the Egyptians, and Israel believes the LORD and Moses.

Exodus 15.summary: Moses and Israel sing to the LORD, who "hath triumphed gloriously" over Pharaoh's army (Exodus 15:1–18). Miriam leads the women with timbrels and dancing (Exodus 15:19–21). Three days later, the water at Marah is bitter, and God shows Moses a tree that makes it sweet (Exodus 15:22–26). The people camp at Elim, with its twelve wells and seventy palm trees (Exodus 15:27).
Exodus 15.whereWeAre: Israel has just walked through the sea on dry ground, and the Egyptian army is gone. The people celebrate with a song. Then reality sets in: three days into the desert they find no good water, and the complaining of the wilderness years begins, continuing in chapter 16.

keyFigures.name: Moses
keyFigures.role: Leads Israel's song and cries to the LORD at Marah.

keyFigures.name: Miriam
keyFigures.role: The prophetess, who leads the women with timbrels and dancing.

keyFigures.name: The people
keyFigures.role: Sing of their rescue, then complain about the bitter water.

keyFigures.name: God
keyFigures.role: Makes the water sweet and calls himself "the LORD that healeth thee."

keyThemes.explanation: Israel sings that the LORD "hath triumphed gloriously."
Miriam and the women sing and dance before the LORD.
God makes the bitter water sweet and calls himself "the LORD that healeth thee."

Exodus 16.summary: In the wilderness of Sin, the people complain that they had more food in Egypt (Exodus 16:1–3). God promises "bread from heaven," and Moses and Aaron tell the people the LORD has heard them (Exodus 16:4–12). Quail come in the evening and manna in the morning, and each person gathers just enough (Exodus 16:13–21). On the sixth day they gather twice as much so they can rest on the Sabbath (Exodus 16:22–30). A jar of manna is kept as a reminder, and Israel eats manna for forty years (Exodus 16:31–36).
Exodus 16.whereWeAre: About a month after leaving Egypt, the people run out of food. They complain, and God sends quail and manna, bread from heaven. Chapter 17 brings the next test, a lack of water.

keyFigures.name: The children of Israel
keyFigures.role: Complain of hunger, then gather manna each morning.

keyFigures.name: Moses and Aaron
keyFigures.role: Tell the people that the LORD has heard them.

keyFigures.name: God
keyFigures.role: Sends quail and manna and teaches Israel to rest on the Sabbath.

keyFigures.name: Some of the people
keyFigures.role: Keep manna overnight or go out to gather on the Sabbath, against God's word.

keyThemes.explanation: God sends manna each morning, and everyone has just enough.
Manna kept overnight rots, but a double share on the sixth day keeps for the Sabbath.
A jar of manna is kept so later generations can see the bread God gave.

explainedReferences.explanation: The manna account about gathering without excess or lack.

Exodus 17.summary: At Rephidim there is no water, and the people quarrel with Moses, so God tells him to strike a rock at Horeb, and water flows (Exodus 17:1–7). Amalek attacks, and Israel wins while Aaron and Hur hold up Moses' hands (Exodus 17:8–13). God tells Moses to write the victory in a book, and Moses builds an altar called Jehovahnissi (Exodus 17:14–16).
Exodus 17.whereWeAre: God has just given manna in chapter 16, but now there is no water. The people quarrel, and God brings water from a rock. Then Israel fights its first battle, against Amalek, before Moses' father-in-law arrives in chapter 18.

keyFigures.name: The people
keyFigures.role: Quarrel with Moses because there is no water.

keyFigures.name: Moses
keyFigures.role: Strikes the rock and holds up the rod during the battle.

keyFigures.name: Joshua
keyFigures.role: Leads Israel's men against Amalek.

keyFigures.name: Aaron and Hur
keyFigures.role: Hold up Moses' hands until sunset.

keyFigures.name: Amalek
keyFigures.role: Attacks Israel at Rephidim.

keyFigures.name: God
keyFigures.role: Brings water from the rock and promises to blot out Amalek.

keyThemes.explanation: The people test God, asking, "Is the LORD among us, or not?"
Aaron and Hur hold up Moses' hands until the battle is won.
Moses builds an altar and names it Jehovahnissi to remember the victory.

Exodus 18.summary: Jethro brings Moses' wife and sons to the camp, rejoices at all God has done, and offers sacrifices (Exodus 18:1–12). Watching Moses judge the people from morning to evening, Jethro advises him to choose able men to judge the smaller cases (Exodus 18:13–23). Moses does as he says, and Jethro goes home (Exodus 18:24–27).
Exodus 18.whereWeAre: Israel has come through the sea, hunger, thirst, and battle, and is camped near the mountain of God. Moses' father-in-law, Jethro, visits and helps him organize the people. In chapter 19 Israel arrives at Mount Sinai, and the story shifts from escape to covenant.

keyFigures.name: Jethro
keyFigures.role: Brings Moses' family, praises the LORD, and gives wise advice.

keyFigures.name: Moses
keyFigures.role: Tells Jethro all God has done and takes his advice.

keyFigures.name: Zipporah and her sons
keyFigures.role: Moses' wife and his sons Gershom and Eliezer, brought to the camp.

keyFigures.name: Aaron and the elders
keyFigures.role: Eat bread with Jethro before God.

keyFigures.name: The new judges
keyFigures.role: Able men set over thousands, hundreds, fifties, and tens.

keyThemes.explanation: Moses listens to Jethro and changes how he leads.
Faithful men judge the small cases so that Moses can handle the hard ones.
Jethro says, "Now I know that the LORD is greater than all gods."

Exodus 19.summary: In the third month after leaving Egypt, Israel camps before Mount Sinai, and God calls them to be "a kingdom of priests, and an holy nation" (Exodus 19:1–6). The people answer, "All that the LORD hath spoken we will do" (Exodus 19:7–8). For three days they wash their clothes and keep away from the mountain (Exodus 19:9–15). Then the LORD comes down on Sinai in fire, with thunder, lightning, smoke, and a loud trumpet (Exodus 19:16–25).
Exodus 19.whereWeAre: Three months after leaving Egypt, Israel reaches Mount Sinai. God saved them from slavery; now he invites them to be his own people. This chapter prepares them for God to speak the Ten Commandments in chapter 20.

keyFigures.name: God
keyFigures.role: Calls Israel to be his own people and comes down on Sinai in fire.

keyFigures.name: Moses
keyFigures.role: Carries God's words to the people and their answer back to God.

keyFigures.name: The children of Israel
keyFigures.role: Agree to obey, prepare for three days, and tremble at the mountain.

keyThemes.explanation: God calls Israel "a peculiar treasure" and "a kingdom of priests, and an holy nation."
The people wash and keep away from the mountain for three days.
Thunder, fire, smoke, and a trumpet show how great and holy God is.

Exodus 20.summary: God speaks the Ten Commandments, beginning with the reminder that he brought Israel out of Egypt (Exodus 20:1–17). The people are afraid and ask Moses to speak to them instead, and Moses goes near the thick darkness where God is (Exodus 20:18–21). God gives rules for simple altars of earth or uncut stone (Exodus 20:22–26).
Exodus 20.whereWeAre: Israel is camped at Mount Sinai and watched God come down on the mountain in fire and smoke in chapter 19. Now God speaks the Ten Commandments. They are the heart of the covenant, and chapters 21–23 show how they apply to daily life.

keyFigures.name: God
keyFigures.role: Speaks the Ten Commandments from Sinai.

keyFigures.name: Moses
keyFigures.role: Draws near to the thick darkness where God is.

keyFigures.name: The people
keyFigures.role: Hear the commands and ask Moses to speak to them instead.

keyThemes.explanation: The commands begin with God's rescue and with having no other gods.
The rest of the commands protect family, life, marriage, property, and the truth.
Israel is to keep the Sabbath and fear God so that they do not sin.

explainedReferences.explanation: The second commandment repeats God's prohibition of bowing to or serving idols.
The second commandment repeats God's promise of mercy to those who love him and keep his commandments.
Repeated commandment: honoring one's father and mother. Also found in Deuteronomy 5:16.
The commandment to honor father and mother and its promise.

The command to honor father and mother.
Repeated commandment: identical prohibition against killing. Also found in Deuteronomy 5:17.
The command against murder is explicitly repeated.

The commandment not to kill.
The command against murder is explicitly repeated.
Repeated commandment: prohibition against adultery. Also found in Deuteronomy 5:18.
The commandment against adultery.
Repeated commandment: identical prohibition against stealing. Also found in Deuteronomy 5:19.
Repeated commandment: forbid bearing false witness. Also found in Deuteronomy 5:20.
Repeated commandment: forbid coveting what belongs to a neighbor. Also found in Deuteronomy 5:21.
The commandment not to covet.

Exodus 21.summary: God gives laws for Hebrew servants, who go free in the seventh year, and for women sold as servants (Exodus 21:1–11). He sets penalties for murder, kidnapping, and injuries, separating deliberate killing from accidents and making the penalty fit the harm (Exodus 21:12–27). An owner is responsible for a dangerous ox or an open pit (Exodus 21:28–36). Some of these laws fit an ancient way of life that can feel strange or troubling to modern readers.
Exodus 21.whereWeAre: God has just given the Ten Commandments in chapter 20. Chapters 21–23 apply them to everyday cases, starting here with servants, violence, and injuries. These laws are called "the book of the covenant" (Exodus 24:7), which Israel agrees to in chapter 24.

keyFigures.name: God
keyFigures.role: Gives Moses laws that apply the Ten Commandments to daily life.

keyFigures.name: Moses
keyFigures.role: Receives "the judgments" he is to set before the people.

keyThemes.explanation: A Hebrew servant goes free in the seventh year.
The law separates murder from accidents, and the penalty must fit the injury.
An owner who knows his ox is dangerous must answer for the harm it does.

explainedReferences.explanation: Concerning cursing one's father or mother.
The legal formula eye for eye and tooth for tooth.

Exodus 22.summary: Laws cover theft, damage to crops, and property left in someone's care (Exodus 22:1–15). Other laws deal with seduction, sorcery, and sacrifice to other gods (Exodus 22:16–20). God warns that he will hear the cry of the stranger, the widow, and the orphan if they are mistreated (Exodus 22:21–24). Loans to the poor must not be used to exploit them (Exodus 22:25–27), and Israel must honor God and give him its firstfruits and firstborn (Exodus 22:28–31).
Exodus 22.whereWeAre: The laws that began in chapter 21 continue. This chapter covers stolen property, damages, and loans, and it gives special protection to strangers, widows, and orphans. Chapter 23 finishes this section of laws.

keyFigures.name: God
keyFigures.role: Continues the laws and promises to hear the cry of widows and orphans.

keyFigures.name: Moses
keyFigures.role: Receives these laws on the mountain.

keyThemes.explanation: A thief or careless neighbor must pay back what was lost.
God warns that he will hear the cry of the stranger, the widow, and the orphan.
A poor man's coat taken as a pledge must be returned by sunset.

Exodus 23.summary: God commands honest witnesses, fair judges, and kindness even to an enemy's animal (Exodus 23:1–9). The land rests every seventh year, and people and animals rest every seventh day (Exodus 23:10–13). Israel gathers for three feasts each year (Exodus 23:14–19). God promises to send an angel ahead of them and to drive out the nations of Canaan, but Israel must not worship their gods (Exodus 23:20–33).
Exodus 23.whereWeAre: This chapter finishes the laws that began in chapter 21. It covers fair courts, rest for the land and for workers, and three yearly feasts. It ends with God's promise to lead Israel into the land, and in chapter 24 the people formally accept the covenant.

keyFigures.name: God
keyFigures.role: Finishes these laws and promises to send an angel ahead of Israel.

keyFigures.name: Moses
keyFigures.role: Receives these laws on the mountain.

keyThemes.explanation: Witnesses and judges must not lie, take bribes, or play favorites.
Israel rests every seventh day and every seventh year and gathers for three feasts.
God will lead them, but they must not worship the gods of the land.

Exodus 24.summary: God calls Moses, Aaron, Nadab, Abihu, and seventy elders to come up and worship (Exodus 24:1–2). Moses reads the book of the covenant, the people promise to obey, and he sprinkles them with "the blood of the covenant" (Exodus 24:3–8). The elders see the God of Israel and eat and drink before him (Exodus 24:9–11). Then Moses goes up into the cloud and stays on the mountain forty days and forty nights (Exodus 24:12–18).
Exodus 24.whereWeAre: God has given the Ten Commandments and the laws of chapters 21–23. Now Israel formally agrees to the covenant, sealed with sacrifice and a meal before God. Moses then climbs the mountain for forty days, where he receives the plans for the tabernacle in chapters 25–31.

keyFigures.name: Moses
keyFigures.role: Writes down the laws, reads them to the people, and climbs into the cloud.

keyFigures.name: The people
keyFigures.role: Promise, "All the words which the LORD hath said will we do."

keyFigures.name: Aaron, Nadab, Abihu, and the seventy elders
keyFigures.role: Go partway up the mountain, see the God of Israel, and eat and drink.

keyFigures.name: Joshua
keyFigures.role: Goes up the mountain with Moses.

keyFigures.name: God
keyFigures.role: Calls Moses up to receive the tables of stone.

keyThemes.explanation: The people agree to the covenant, and Moses seals it with blood.
The elders see the God of Israel and eat and drink before him.
Moses goes into the cloud and stays forty days.

Exodus 25.summary: God asks the people for willing gifts so that they can build a sanctuary where he will dwell among them (Exodus 25:1–9). He gives the plan for the ark and its mercy seat, with two cherubims of gold (Exodus 25:10–22). He describes the table for the showbread (Exodus 25:23–30) and the lampstand of pure gold, telling Moses to follow the pattern he was shown (Exodus 25:31–40). This begins a long section about the design and building of the tabernacle, God's tent.
Exodus 25.whereWeAre: Moses is on the mountain for forty days after the covenant ceremony in chapter 24. God begins giving him plans for the tabernacle, a tent where God will live among his people. This chapter covers the ark, the table, and the lampstand, and the plans continue through chapter 31.

keyFigures.name: God
keyFigures.role: Asks for willing gifts and gives Moses the plan for the ark, the table, and the lampstand.

keyFigures.name: Moses
keyFigures.role: Receives the pattern on the mountain.

keyThemes.explanation: The tabernacle is built from gifts given "willingly with his heart."
God says, "let them make me a sanctuary; that I may dwell among them."
Everything must be made like the pattern God shows Moses.

explainedReferences.explanation: Instruction to make the tabernacle according to the pattern shown.

Exodus 26.summary: God describes the curtains of fine linen with cherubims, and the coverings of goats' hair and skins (Exodus 26:1–14). The tent stands on boards set in silver sockets and held by bars (Exodus 26:15–30). A veil divides the holy place from the most holy place, where the ark will stand (Exodus 26:31–37).
Exodus 26.whereWeAre: In chapter 25 God described the furniture for the tabernacle. Now he describes the tent itself: its curtains, its frames, and the veil that closes off the most holy place. Chapter 27 moves outside to the altar and the courtyard.

keyFigures.name: God
keyFigures.role: Gives the plan for the tent, its frames, and the veil.

keyFigures.name: Moses
keyFigures.role: Is told to set up the tabernacle by the pattern he was shown.

keyThemes.explanation: A veil separates the most holy place, where the ark will stand.
Every curtain, board, and socket is measured.
The frames can be taken apart and carried as Israel travels.

Exodus 27.summary: God describes a bronze altar for burnt offerings, with horns on its corners and poles to carry it (Exodus 27:1–8). A courtyard of linen hangings surrounds the tabernacle (Exodus 27:9–19). The people are to bring pure olive oil, and Aaron and his sons must keep the lamp burning before the LORD (Exodus 27:20–21).
Exodus 27.whereWeAre: Chapter 26 described the tent of the tabernacle. Now the plans move outside, to the bronze altar and the courtyard around it. Chapter 28 turns from the building to the priests who will serve there.

keyFigures.name: God
keyFigures.role: Gives the plan for the altar and the courtyard.

keyFigures.name: Moses
keyFigures.role: Is told to have the people bring oil for the lamp.

keyFigures.name: Aaron and his sons
keyFigures.role: Charged to keep the lamp burning before the LORD.

keyThemes.explanation: The altar and courtyard show the way into God's presence.
The lamp is to burn before the LORD from evening to morning.
The people bring the oil, and the priests tend the lamp.

Exodus 28.summary: God chooses Aaron and his sons as priests and tells Moses to have skilled workers make holy garments (Exodus 28:1–5). The ephod carries two stones engraved with the names of the tribes (Exodus 28:6–14). The breastplate holds twelve stones for the twelve tribes, with the Urim and the Thummim (Exodus 28:15–30). Aaron's robe has bells and pomegranates on its hem (Exodus 28:31–35), and his turban bears a gold plate reading "HOLINESS TO THE LORD" (Exodus 28:36–38). Coats, sashes, and caps are made for his sons (Exodus 28:39–43).
Exodus 28.whereWeAre: The plans for the tabernacle itself were finished in chapters 25–27. Now God chooses Aaron and his sons as priests and describes the clothes they will wear. Chapter 29 explains how they will be set apart for this work.

keyFigures.name: God
keyFigures.role: Chooses Aaron and his sons as priests and describes their garments.

keyFigures.name: Moses
keyFigures.role: Is told to bring Aaron near and have the garments made.

keyFigures.name: Aaron
keyFigures.role: Will carry the names of the tribes on his shoulders and over his heart.

keyFigures.name: Aaron's sons
keyFigures.role: Nadab, Abihu, Eleazar, and Ithamar, chosen to serve as priests.

keyFigures.name: The skilled workers
keyFigures.role: Filled with "the spirit of wisdom" to make the garments.

keyThemes.explanation: Aaron wears the tribes' names over his heart when he goes before the LORD.
The gold plate on Aaron's turban shows that the priests belong to God.
Craftsmen use their God-given skill to make garments "for glory and for beauty."

Exodus 29.summary: God explains how Aaron and his sons will be set apart: washing, dressing, anointing, and sacrifices over seven days (Exodus 29:1–37). A lamb is to be offered every morning and every evening (Exodus 29:38–42). God promises to meet with Israel and to "dwell among the children of Israel" (Exodus 29:43–46).
Exodus 29.whereWeAre: Chapter 28 described the priests' clothes. This chapter explains the seven-day ceremony that will set Aaron and his sons apart as priests. It ends with God's promise to live among Israel, and chapter 30 adds the last items for the tabernacle.

keyFigures.name: God
keyFigures.role: Gives the ceremony that sets the priests apart and promises to live among Israel.

keyFigures.name: Moses
keyFigures.role: Is told to wash, clothe, and anoint the priests.

keyFigures.name: Aaron and his sons
keyFigures.role: The priests to be set apart over seven days.

keyThemes.explanation: Washing, new clothes, oil, and sacrifices make the priests ready.
A lamb is offered every morning and every evening.
God promises, "I will dwell among the children of Israel."

Exodus 30.summary: God describes a golden altar for burning incense every morning and evening (Exodus 30:1–10). Every man counted in a census gives half a shekel, rich and poor alike (Exodus 30:11–16). A bronze basin is made for the priests to wash in (Exodus 30:17–21). God gives recipes for the holy anointing oil (Exodus 30:22–33) and the holy incense, which must never be made for personal use (Exodus 30:34–38).
Exodus 30.whereWeAre: The priests and their ordination were described in chapters 28–29. Now God adds the last pieces of the plan: the incense altar, a census offering, a washing basin, and special oil and incense. Chapter 31 names the craftsmen and ends Moses' forty days on the mountain.

keyFigures.name: God
keyFigures.role: Gives the last plans: the incense altar, the census offering, the basin, and the holy oil and incense.

keyFigures.name: Moses
keyFigures.role: Receives these instructions.

keyFigures.name: Aaron
keyFigures.role: Will burn incense every morning and evening.

keyThemes.explanation: Incense rises before God every morning and evening.
Rich and poor give the same half shekel.
The holy oil and incense must never be copied for ordinary use.

Exodus 31.summary: God fills Bezaleel of Judah with his Spirit and gives him Aholiab of Dan to lead the work on the tabernacle (Exodus 31:1–11). He repeats that the Sabbath is a sign between him and Israel forever (Exodus 31:12–17). Then he gives Moses "two tables of testimony" written "with the finger of God" (Exodus 31:18).
Exodus 31.whereWeAre: This is the last of the tabernacle instructions that began in chapter 25. God names the craftsmen, repeats the Sabbath command, and gives Moses the two stone tablets. But while Moses has been on the mountain, the people below have been busy, as chapter 32 reveals.

keyFigures.name: God
keyFigures.role: Fills Bezaleel with his Spirit, repeats the Sabbath, and gives Moses the tablets.

keyFigures.name: Bezaleel
keyFigures.role: Of the tribe of Judah, chosen to lead the work.

keyFigures.name: Aholiab
keyFigures.role: Of the tribe of Dan, chosen to work with him.

keyFigures.name: Moses
keyFigures.role: Receives "two tables of testimony" written by God.

keyThemes.explanation: God fills Bezaleel with his Spirit for skilled work.
The Sabbath is "a sign between me and you" for all generations.
The tablets are "written with the finger of God."

Exodus 32.summary: While Moses is on the mountain, the people ask Aaron to make them gods, and he makes a golden calf (Exodus 32:1–6). God tells Moses what they have done, and Moses pleads for them (Exodus 32:7–14). Moses comes down, breaks the tablets, and burns the calf (Exodus 32:15–20). Aaron makes excuses (Exodus 32:21–24), and the Levites answer Moses' call and kill about three thousand men (Exodus 32:25–29). Moses offers his own life for the people's sin, and the LORD sends a plague (Exodus 32:30–35).
Exodus 32.whereWeAre: Moses has been on the mountain for forty days receiving God's plans in chapters 25–31. Meanwhile, the people grow tired of waiting and make a golden calf. Only weeks after promising to obey, they break the covenant, and chapters 33–34 ask whether God will still go with them.

keyFigures.name: The people
keyFigures.role: Grow tired of waiting and demand gods to go before them.

keyFigures.name: Aaron
keyFigures.role: Makes the golden calf and builds an altar before it.

keyFigures.name: God
keyFigures.role: Tells Moses what the people have done and threatens to destroy them.

keyFigures.name: Moses
keyFigures.role: Pleads for Israel, breaks the tablets, and offers his own life for them.

keyFigures.name: Joshua
keyFigures.role: Hears the noise from the camp and thinks it is war.

keyFigures.name: The Levites
keyFigures.role: Answer Moses' call and go through the camp with swords.

keyThemes.explanation: While Moses is away, the people make a golden calf and call it their god.
Moses pleads for the people and even offers his own life for them.
Moses breaks the tablets, a sign that the covenant has been broken.

explainedReferences.explanation: Israel eating, drinking, and rising to play.

Exodus 33.summary: God tells Israel to go on to the land but says he will not go with them himself, and the people mourn and take off their ornaments (Exodus 33:1–6). Moses meets the LORD in a tent outside the camp, where God speaks with him "face to face" (Exodus 33:7–11). Moses pleads for God's presence to go with them, and God agrees (Exodus 33:12–17). When Moses asks to see God's glory, God covers him with his hand so that he sees only God's back (Exodus 33:18–23).
Exodus 33.whereWeAre: The golden calf in chapter 32 has broken the covenant, and God says he will not go with Israel himself. Moses pleads with God to stay with his people. God agrees and promises to show Moses his glory, which happens in chapter 34.

keyFigures.name: God
keyFigures.role: Says he will not go with Israel, then agrees after Moses pleads.

keyFigures.name: Moses
keyFigures.role: Speaks with God "face to face" and asks to see his glory.

keyFigures.name: The people
keyFigures.role: Mourn and take off their ornaments.

keyFigures.name: Joshua
keyFigures.role: Stays in the tent where Moses meets with God.

keyThemes.explanation: Moses says, "If thy presence go not with me, carry us not up hence."
The people mourn and take off their ornaments.
Moses may see God's goodness pass by, but no one can see his face and live.

explainedReferences.explanation: Words about having mercy and compassion.

Exodus 34.summary: Moses cuts two new tablets, and the LORD passes by, proclaiming that he is "merciful and gracious, longsuffering" (Exodus 34:1–9). God renews the covenant and its commands about worship, the feasts, and the firstborn, and Moses spends forty more days on the mountain (Exodus 34:10–28). When he comes down, his face shines, so he wears a veil after speaking God's words to the people (Exodus 34:29–35).
Exodus 34.whereWeAre: Moses broke the first stone tablets in chapter 32 and pleaded with God in chapter 33. Now God gives new tablets and renews the covenant. Moses comes down with a shining face, and in chapter 35 the building of the tabernacle begins.

keyFigures.name: God
keyFigures.role: Passes by Moses, proclaims his name, and renews the covenant.

keyFigures.name: Moses
keyFigures.role: Cuts new tablets, spends forty days on the mountain, and comes down with a shining face.

keyFigures.name: Aaron and the people
keyFigures.role: Are afraid to come near Moses at first.

keyThemes.explanation: God calls himself "merciful and gracious, longsuffering," yet he will not clear the guilty.
God renews the covenant and warns Israel against other gods.
Time with God leaves Moses' face shining.

explainedReferences.explanation: Description of himself as longsuffering, merciful, and forgiving in his intercession.

Exodus 35.summary: Moses repeats the Sabbath command (Exodus 35:1–3), then asks everyone "of a willing heart" to bring gifts for the tabernacle (Exodus 35:4–19). Men and women bring gold, cloth, skins, wood, and spices, and skilled women spin yarn (Exodus 35:20–29). Moses names Bezaleel and Aholiab as the master craftsmen and teachers (Exodus 35:30–35).
Exodus 35.whereWeAre: The covenant has been renewed after the golden calf in chapters 32–34. Now Israel finally starts to build the tabernacle God described in chapters 25–31. The people bring gifts, and the work continues through chapter 40.

keyFigures.name: Moses
keyFigures.role: Gathers Israel, repeats the Sabbath, and calls for gifts.

keyFigures.name: The people
keyFigures.role: Bring gifts with willing hearts.

keyFigures.name: The skilled women
keyFigures.role: Spin blue, purple, and scarlet yarn, fine linen, and goats' hair.

keyFigures.name: The rulers
keyFigures.role: Bring onyx stones, spices, and oil.

keyFigures.name: Bezaleel and Aholiab
keyFigures.role: Named by Moses as the master craftsmen and teachers.

keyThemes.explanation: Even holy work stops on the Sabbath.
Everyone "of a willing heart" brings a gift.
God gives different people different skills for one task.

Exodus 36.summary: The people bring so many gifts that the workers tell Moses there is more than enough, and he stops the giving (Exodus 36:1–7). The craftsmen make the curtains and coverings (Exodus 36:8–19), the boards and bars (Exodus 36:20–34), and the veil and the door hanging (Exodus 36:35–38).
Exodus 36.whereWeAre: In chapter 35 the people began bringing gifts for the tabernacle. They bring so much that Moses has to tell them to stop. Then the craftsmen make the curtains and frames, and chapter 37 turns to the furniture.

keyFigures.name: Bezaleel and Aholiab
keyFigures.role: Lead the craftsmen in the work.

keyFigures.name: The skilled workers
keyFigures.role: Tell Moses that the people have brought too much.

keyFigures.name: Moses
keyFigures.role: Sends word through the camp to stop the giving.

keyFigures.name: The people
keyFigures.role: Keep bringing gifts every morning.

keyThemes.explanation: The people give so much that Moses has to stop them.
Moses stops the gifts once there is enough.
The workers make every piece just as God commanded.

Exodus 37.summary: Bezaleel makes the ark and the mercy seat with its cherubims (Exodus 37:1–9) and the table for the showbread (Exodus 37:10–16). He makes the lampstand of pure gold, with its flowers and buds (Exodus 37:17–24), and the altar of incense, the holy oil, and the incense (Exodus 37:25–29). Everything follows the designs God gave Moses in chapters 25–30.
Exodus 37.whereWeAre: The tent's curtains and frames were made in chapter 36. Now Bezaleel makes the furniture for the inside: the ark, the table, the lampstand, and the incense altar. Chapter 38 moves out to the altar and the courtyard.

keyFigures.name: Bezaleel
keyFigures.role: Makes the ark, the mercy seat, the table, the lampstand, and the incense altar.

keyThemes.explanation: The furniture is made exactly as God described.
The ark, table, lampstand, and altar are the center of Israel's worship.
The lampstand is made of pure gold, with flowers and buds.

Exodus 38.summary: The workers make the bronze altar (Exodus 38:1–7) and the bronze basin, from mirrors given by the women who served at the tabernacle door (Exodus 38:8). They make the courtyard and its hangings (Exodus 38:9–20). Then the gold, silver, and bronze are counted under Ithamar, Aaron's son (Exodus 38:21–31). Every gift is counted, showing the work was done honestly.
Exodus 38.whereWeAre: The furniture inside the tabernacle was made in chapter 37. This chapter makes the bronze altar, the washing basin, and the courtyard, and it counts the metals used. Chapter 39 finishes with the priests' clothes.

keyFigures.name: Bezaleel
keyFigures.role: Makes the bronze altar, the basin, and the courtyard.

keyFigures.name: Aholiab
keyFigures.role: Works with him as an engraver and embroiderer.

keyFigures.name: The women at the tabernacle door
keyFigures.role: Give their bronze mirrors for the basin.

keyFigures.name: Ithamar
keyFigures.role: Aaron's son, who leads the Levites in counting the metals.

keyThemes.explanation: The bronze altar stands in the courtyard.
Women give their mirrors to make the bronze basin.
Every talent of gold, silver, and bronze is counted.

Exodus 39.summary: The workers make the priests' holy garments, the ephod, the breastplate, the robe, and the gold plate, "as the LORD commanded Moses" (Exodus 39:1–31). All the finished work is brought to Moses, who sees that it was done just as commanded and blesses the people (Exodus 39:32–43).
Exodus 39.whereWeAre: The tabernacle and its furniture were made in chapters 36–38. Now the priests' clothes are made, and all the finished work is brought to Moses. He sees it was done just as God commanded, and in chapter 40 the tabernacle is set up.

keyFigures.name: The workers
keyFigures.role: Make the priests' garments and finish all the work.

keyFigures.name: Moses
keyFigures.role: Looks over the finished work and blesses the people.

keyThemes.explanation: Again and again the chapter says the work was done "as the LORD commanded Moses."
The breastplate holds twelve stones for the twelve tribes.
Moses inspects the finished work and blesses the people.

Exodus 40.summary: God tells Moses to set up the tabernacle on the first day of the first month and to anoint Aaron and his sons as priests (Exodus 40:1–15). Moses sets up the tent and puts everything in its place, doing "according to all that the LORD commanded him" (Exodus 40:16–33). Then the cloud covers the tent, and the glory of the LORD fills the tabernacle so that Moses cannot enter (Exodus 40:34–35). From then on, Israel travels when the cloud lifts and stays when it rests (Exodus 40:36–38).
Exodus 40.whereWeAre: All the pieces of the tabernacle were finished and checked in chapter 39. Now Moses sets it up, and "the glory of the LORD filled the tabernacle" (Exodus 40:34). Exodus ends with God living among his people, and Leviticus begins with God speaking to Moses from this tent.

keyFigures.name: God
keyFigures.role: Tells Moses to set up the tabernacle and fills it with his glory.

keyFigures.name: Moses
keyFigures.role: Sets up the tabernacle, doing "according to all that the LORD commanded him."

keyFigures.name: Aaron and his sons
keyFigures.role: Washed, clothed, and anointed as priests.

keyFigures.name: The children of Israel
keyFigures.role: Travel when the cloud lifts and stay when it rests.

keyThemes.explanation: Moses sets up everything just as God commanded.
The glory of the LORD fills the tabernacle so that even Moses cannot enter.
The cloud tells Israel when to travel and when to stay.
